madam president, the presumption of innocence is a fundamental element of criminal procedure in a democracy with a fair judicial system. we in europe have a unique opportunity to demonstrate to the world the direction of the development of criminal law and the procedural rights of the accused. i consider it a major achievement that the presumption of innocence will apply at all stages from the moment a person is suspected or accused of having committed a crime to the final determination of whether the person has committed the crime in question and the final confirmation of that determination. this will ensure the utmost fairness of the proceedings for the accused and their opportunity for adequate protection, which is the aim of this proposal. another major achievement of the directive is that it prohibits public authorities from ruling in advance on the guilt of a person without thereby impeding the work of the public prosecutor's office. only the court can determine guilt based on the evidence presented to it. last but not least, i welcome the fact that suspects should not be presented in a way that makes them look guilty. the way in which it is presented can greatly influence public sentiment, which is what the directive aims to avoid. at the same time, the restriction of the movement of suspects for security reasons or in case of threat to escape should not be prevented. i believe that minimum rules at european level on the presumption of innocence and the rights attached to this principle will contribute to ensuring the right to a fair trial, to strengthening mutual trust and to the effective application of the principle of mutual recognition.

in writing. i voted in favour of this report because it represents an important step towards completing the existing european legal framework on the rights of defence of suspects, accused persons or persons subject to criminal proceedings within the european union. this proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council is of key importance because, at present, in many eu member states, the protection of the rights of suspects and accused persons is undermined and the principle of the presumption of innocence is violated. the presumption of innocence is a fundamental legal principle which makes it possible to avoid abuses in the course of criminal proceedings. the adoption of this report aims to strengthen the right of suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings throughout the european union to the presumption of innocence pending a final verdict of guilty and to guarantee the right of persons to be present at the trial against them.

president-in-office of the council.– mr president, on this occasion, ten weeks after the paris terrorist attacks, i would like to be able to say that most probably we will never again witness such a heinous attack in europe. unfortunately, i am not convinced that this is true. on the contrary, judging from recent events, the terrorist threat seems to be increasing in the european union, but also in its vicinity and further afield, as the recent attacks in istanbul, jakarta, ouagadougou and charsadda in pakistan have shown. as the presidency, we will do everything within our powers to improve the union’s capacity to counter this threat and to protect our citizens. in this context, counter—terrorism will be a key topic at the informal meeting of the justice and home affairs ministers next week in amsterdam. the presidency also attaches great importance to the rule of law and to getting the balance right in this respect in the fight against terrorism. obstacles to the exchange of information on foreign terrorist fighters and the way forward to clear these obstacles will be first and foremost on the agenda. another issue that we will address is information sharing between member states on firearms and explosive precursors. implementation of the measures agreed is key, as indicated in the eu internal security strategy 2015-2020. the heads of state and government statement on counter-terrorism of 12 february 2015, after the charlie hebdo attacks, remains the framework the european union needs to implement urgently, as called for by the european council. you can be assured that the presidency will spare no effort to promote rapid progress in its implementation. progress has been made over the past months and was set out in a public report by the european union counter—terrorism coordinator in late november. information sharing and operational cooperation are top priorities identified by the council. progress has been made. the agreement on the european union pnr directive will support police and intelligence agencies in tracking down possible terrorists and criminals by accessing travel details of passengers. on 1 january, europol launched the european counter—terrorism centre (ectc). this is a more robust platform through which member states can increase information sharing and operational coordination. this includes the monitoring and investigation of foreign terrorist fighters, as well as the trafficking of illegal firearms and terrorist financing. in november 2015 member states committed to seconding counter-terrorism (ct) experts to the ectc to form an enhanced cross-border investigation support unit. europol is actively engaged in supporting ongoing ct investigations in several member states. the progress of contributions to the various eu databases is being monitored and discussed in the council. outside the european union context, cooperation and information sharing among security services will be stepped up in the context of the counter terrorist group (ctg), and the commission will soon present its proposal on updating the european criminal records information system for the systematic sharing of criminal records data for people connected to terrorism. furthermore, we have started discussing the proposal to amend to framework decision on combating terrorism. on 2 december 2015, the commission presented a draft directive with a view to collectively implementing un security council resolution 2178 and the additional protocol to the council of europe convention. negotiations on this directive are already under way and we hope to be in a position to achieve an agreement in june this year. apart from enhancing the exchange of law enforcement information, countering radicalisation and recruitment remains a priority. an eu approach is needed, taking into account that over 5 000 citizens have left to fight for terrorist organisations in iraq and syria. concerning integration and non-discrimination, we should create opportunities for all. we should do much more on tolerance and anti-muslim hatred, further inter-religious dialogue and communicate our values. education is key and we look forward to commission initiatives in this context. but prevention alone is not enough. the return of well—trained radicalised individuals poses a genuine security threat. at european union level, the main tool we have for sharing best practices is the radicalisation awareness network. this network has made impressive strides in recent months, facilitating the flow of best practice and expertise between member states. we can also begin to share expertise with third countries. the immediate focus here will be the middle east, the north africa region and turkey. it is a fact that the internet is one of the primary channels for radicalisation, publishing and proliferating illegal content. the establishment of an internet referral unit within europol’s counter—terrorism centre has improved our ability to obtain the removal of terrorist threats. on 3 december 2015 the eu internet forum was launched. the objective is to identify and remove terrorist content and to develop effective counter-narratives. in this context, cooperation with the providers is obviously important. the discussion of the commission’s proposal for an eu action plan against illicit trafficking in and use of firearms and explosives has begun. the presidency aims to reach a general approach on this new proposal. finally, i would like to mention the border police package, which is also important in the context of the fight against terrorism, as we have to strengthen controls at the eu’s external borders. border security is not a top priority under our presidency. on this issue one should of course be careful about mixing migration and terrorism. we cannot turn our eyes away from the threat, but let us not forget that the vast majority of migrants are fleeing situations of conflict and even fleeing from terrorism themselves. the close cooperation with key partners, such as the united states, is continuing. furthermore, we will continue to strengthen our counter-terrorism engagement with partners in north africa, the middle east, turkey and the western balkans. let me conclude by saying that i think we all share the same objectives. among other things, this was demonstrated by your resolution of february last year on anti-terrorism and the reports adopted by the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs at the end of last year. we look forward to a fruitful cooperation.

and too many lives scarred. we have to be realistic: the terrorist threat in the european union is high. the terrorist threat is there. we are determined to respond with resolve and resilience, and at the same time to uphold our values of tolerance, democracy and respect for fundamental rights. from day one of this commission, we stressed that combating terrorism was a common european responsibility. our european agenda on security has been on the table, as you know, since last april. we have drastically accelerated its delivery with the political agreement on the eu pnr, the proposal for a directive on terrorism, the november firearms package, the action plan on firearms trafficking, the europol regulation adopted in december, the reinforced ran centre of excellence to counter radicalisation, the launch of the eu internet forum to counter harmful content online and, just this week, the proposal to exchange the criminal records of non-eu nationals. these are all tangible measures to strengthen our security across borders, and more is coming. 2016 will be the year when we go after terrorist money. we need to deprive terrorists of their financial resources. in early february, we will put our ideas forward with a concrete timetable. our borders package of last december is also a critical piece of the puzzle, because it will allow the systematic security checks of all people leaving and entering the eu. it is clear that we need to improve the management of our external borders in order to enhance internal security and safeguard schengen. i want to be they need to share more information, between themselves and also with europol. law enforcement authorities across member states, including specialised law enforcement agencies, all work for the same purpose: the security of our citizens. we need to understand that, collectively, we are all safer. the threats we face are common. our approaches to the threats need to be common too. this is not a share information. this centre can only succeed in its mission if we all help it to succeed. the support provided by europol to french and belgian investigators after the paris attacks is the best example of the role that the european counter terrorism centre could play: cross-checking data, facilitating information-sharing and providing analytical and operational assistance to the national services on the ground. one year ago, following the charlie hebdo attacks, we stressed that our response would not be dictated by fear or driven by hasty conclusions. the commission proposed several concrete actions which are part of a comprehensive approach, and in this collective effort we have made progress. but recent events remind us that we still need to do much more. now is the time to act and to strengthen our cooperation. let us make 2016 a turning point for europe to tackle terrorism decisively, head-on, in all its aspects.

in writing. ‒ as the shadow rapporteur on the kosovo reports, i welcome and support the conclusion of a stabilisation and association agreement between kosovo and the european union. this agreement is a first step towards the country's european integration and sets out the conditions for participation in european policies and financial instruments. but the right to use european funds is conditional on the country implementing key reforms in the areas of statecraft, the judiciary, the fight against corruption and organised crime. the country is in a difficult institutional situation and that is why it needs guidance and help in building its statehood, and kosovars need jobs and a rise in living standards to stop leaving their country. in addition to access to european funds, the agreement provides for further visa liberalisation, which will take place when kosovo has fulfilled all the conditions set by the european commission.

in writing. ‒ the association agreement/deep and comprehensive free trade agreements with georgia, moldova and ukraine require the parties to implement comprehensive political and economic reforms, in return for preferential access to the union's internal market and improved conditions for cooperation. the resolution in question examines the progress made by these three countries over the past year. the undisputed champion among them is georgia, which will soon get visa liberalisation. but many other democratic issues remain unresolved, such as the independence of the judiciary, freedom of the media and the repression of opposition. moldova is in a severe political crisis that threatens the process of european integration and the implementation of reforms. ukraine is also trying to reform its system and cope with organised crime, corruption and a difficult economic environment. i supported the european parliament's resolution because i believe it comprehensively presents the problems of these countries and provides key recommendations for their reform and european integration process.
in writing. i voted in favour of this resolution because it emphasises the importance of the union's commitment to the eastern partnership countries. in the resolution, we welcome the progress made by ukraine, moldova and georgia and recall that the implementation of the deep and comprehensive association and free trade agreements must remain a priority for the union and these three countries. we welcome the financial and technical assistance provided by the union, while stressing that the financial support of the union must be conditional on concrete reforms, in particular in the areas of justice and the rule of law. finally, it is important to place these agreements within the wider framework of strengthening our partnership, which must cover both political dialogue and priority areas ranging from employment to energy, security, conflict prevention and the fight against terrorism.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the resolution on the common defence clause (article 42 (7) teu) because i believe that security and defence should remain entirely within the competence of the member states and that no further powers in this area should be conferred at eu level. separately, france has no reason to use this article and to ask for a greater engagement of the union in the war in syria, since the eu is not a security and defence organisation but a political and economic union. cooperation in the fight against is and terrorism should be done through nato, which is the most appropriate organisation and to which all member states belong. last but not least, there is concern that the use of article 42 (7) of the french constitution may be used to justify the many breaches of european law in areas such as public procurement, security, the free movement of goods and people, public debt and others.
in writing. i voted in favour of this resolution because it stresses that the use of the mutual defence clause is a sign of the unanimous support of all the member states for france and is, in this sense, a sign of european solidarity, which is the foundation of the union. in the resolution, we deplore the intergovernmental nature of this clause and recall the 'facilitating' role of the european institutions, which can ensure a collective and effective response when this clause is invoked. we ask the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy to propose guidelines on the practical arrangements for this clause, in order to avoid ad hoc management and cooperation in the future. finally, we stress the catalytic role of this first activation, which can serve to lay the foundations for a genuine european defence union.
in writing. ‒ by invoking article 42(7) teu instead of article 222 tfeu (the so-called ‘solidarity clause’), france chose an intra—government approach rather than an institutional one. in this regard, we can conclude that the activation of article 42(7) represents an important test for member states since they are obliged to provide ‘aid and assistance by all means in their power’ to support france. there is no doubt that the best way to pass this test for member states is to take their commitments under article 42(7) teu seriously. this refers to the point that member states should be well prepared not only to provide immediate support (whether it is political, military of financial) but also to bear the cost of such support. moreover, to achieve better application in future applications of article 42(7), member states should use the full potential of the european institutions, especially the eeas and the commission. moreover, this will facilitate cohesion between the eu institutions and member states, which will hopefully result in further integration.
in writing. ‒ the european parliament's joint resolution on eu priorities for the 2016 sessions of the un human rights council sets out the eu's position at the upcoming meeting of the un human rights council in march in geneva. the resolution is comprehensive and addresses thematic issues such as the death penalty, freedom of religion, social and economic rights, and the human rights situation in a number of countries such as saudi arabia, burundi, syria and others. the group of european conservatives and reformists has always placed a high priority on human rights in all eu policies and relations with third countries. however, our group did not join the joint resolution, as it focuses on lgbti rights, which we cannot support, as we promote the preservation of family and christian values. that is why i decided to abstain.
in writing. ‒ i supported the resolution because in a decade the un human rights council has established itself as a platform that identifies and proposes responses to today's human rights challenges. it also serves as a major reference point for human rights research, education, public information, and advocacy activities within the un system. in this perspective, it should not surprise us that a prominent champion of human rights like the eu, which promotes and protects human rights both within the union and beyond its borders, provides comprehensive political and financial support in this direction. it is from the position of a leading political and financial supporter of human rights that the eu must continue to raise and express its concern on the international stage about human rights violations. including some of the council members. i believe it is absolutely essential that basic criteria for membership of the un human rights council be introduced. the parties should be chosen from among those that uphold a high level of human rights. only then can it be ensured that the council exercises its mandate in an effective and impartial manner and is not subjective or dependent.

mr president, i would like to get back to an issue i raised when discussing the previous ecb report, and that is the availability of bank lending to businesses. unfortunately, the situation is still unsatisfactory, despite the measures that have been taken lately. european businesses are largely dependent on bank lending and alternative financial sources are quite insufficient to meet the necessary demand. i do still welcome the measures taken by the ecb to address this problem. these include negative interest rates and targeted long-term refinancing operations. i am also happy to see from the early evidence in this year’s report that parallel policy initiatives were relatively effective, especially when it comes to reducing financial stability risk and giving banks funding. however, while the targeted long-term refinancing operation helped stem the decrease in bank loans, the programme did not provide a stimulus to generate loan growth as intended. a total of eur 400 billion has been introduced into the banking system through five refinancing operations, but bank corporate lending has only experienced a very moderate growth. as the ecb annual report 2014 points out, credit conditions for firms remain tight, especially in some euro area countries. we can see that ecb monetary policies were transmitted only imperfectly to borrowing costs. bank lending is still insufficient at times, and therefore i do ask the commission to take more decisive measures to stimulate bank lending to corporations and, especially, to smes.
the rapporteur. i would like to thank in particular the shadow rapporteurs, as well as the partners from the luxembourg presidency and the commission, for the particularly constructive approach and contributions that made the drafting of this draft decision possible. undeclared work, in its increasingly diverse forms, today deprives those employed of their basic social and labour rights, often putting them in conditions of de facto exploitation, leads to serious market distortions, forcing compliant firms to overcome extremely unfair competition from employers using such work, and deprives tax and social security systems of revenue and payments due. it is to these disadvantaged communities and institutions that we owe the present platform and its early and effective implementation. the need to create this platform is all the more urgent in view of the escalating threats not only to labour mobility but also to one of the four indivisible fundamental freedoms - that of the free movement of people - and to the very existence of the union. and i would like to share the view that it was precisely this sense of urgency, which was increasingly shared by both my fellow parliamentarians and the luxembourg presidency and the commission, that became the driving force behind the achievement of constructive agreement on the final draft resolution presented to parliament today. the compromise thus reached commits all member states to be responsible members of the platform. the platform is intended to enhance the capacity of member states to act on the multiple painful problems posed by undeclared work through enhanced cooperation at union level between relevant national authorities, together with the social partners and with the participation as observers of a wide range of interested agencies and organisations. accordingly, the mission of the platform was defined to prevent, limit and counter undeclared work and to promote the conversion of such work into declared work. the proposed platform, in line with the principle of subsidiarity, will not have the power to establish rules and standards. instead, it is intended to offer the necessary basis for the responsible consideration of information, experience and solutions as a basis for shared conclusions aimed at effectively addressing the challenges of undeclared work. the activities within the scope of the platform shall include a wide range of specific actions in pursuit of its mission. it is up to the individual member states to make use, as appropriate, of the conclusions resulting from such action, and to the institutions of the european union to take account of those of theirs falling within the responsibilities of the union. true, there were doubts is the platform necessary at all, will it not affect the freedom of action of the member states, in fact, is there really room for added value at union level for action to tackle undeclared work? rest assured that the full range of such doubts and reservations were addressed in the most detailed and comprehensive manner possible during the consultations, which allowed a broadly shared consensus to be reached and thus to agree on a mutually acceptable and therefore workable draft solution. as a result, the question ultimately comes down to this: are we truly committed to joining forces in a common cause against the gross injustices of undeclared work, or will the objectors find themselves in a position of benefiting all those who exploit this hired labour and consequently reap profits as a result of extremely unfair competition, while depriving budgets of revenue and payments due. that is, do we seek to enforce the law, or in the predominant cases do we let freedom be governed by the so-called "law of the jungle"? an obvious choice, on which parliament cannot possibly be divided.
madam president, strengthening cooperation at european level to prevent and deter undeclared work is of paramount importance not only for the european economy and its public finances, but also for citizens themselves. undeclared work and undeclared work seriously undermine people's ability to enjoy the social benefits that should be available by default. these include accumulation of insurance and pension years, use of leave for holidays, sickness or maternity leave, and additional pay for overtime work. very often, workers in europe are put in a bind and forced to accept such arrangements. high unemployment rates are further contributing to this. we must therefore welcome measures to tackle this phenomenon and encourage cooperation between member states and between national authorities at central and regional level.
member of the commission. today you will approve the decision to step up the fight against undeclared work and tomorrow, as a colleague has already stressed, you will also vote on the package to combat tax evasion which you will be discussing shortly. those two files reinforce each other. both initiatives are intended to make it clear that europe is a space, that europe is a community based on values and where social justice has its place. both dossiers, including this platform to combat undeclared work, will ensure that there is a better level playing field for the business community - rapporteur.– madam president, i believe that the debate this morning has served a very important purpose. as the commissioner began her initial intervention this morning, she highlighted the particular severity of the complex problem of undeclared work and the corresponding need for clear talking and for very definite and unequivocal conclusions, and she stated further intentions for action. i would like to highlight what i believe has been the underlying conclusion: that the various direct impacts of undeclared work on workers, tax and social security systems, and unfair competition, finally come back down to a threat to the very fabric of society in each of the member states and throughout the european union. if i am not mistaken, yesterday evening president draghi began his intervention by pointing out that, at present, the european union is faced with increasing infringements relating to social cohesion – economic, territorial and social cohesion. it is not by chance, i believe, that he began with that point, because whatever efforts for job creation, investment and fiscal responsibility we want to implement, if the basic fabric of the society in which we are trying to implement such measures is being destroyed, then they are hopelessly forsaken. therefore i believe, as has been pointed out, that this platform has seemingly built an acceptable balance between the concerns for individual member states’ rights and the need for union input so that the problem is better tackled. i see that the time is over. i can only second the intention which was mentioned. we hope the platform is put into action before the summer. we very much support the statement by commissioner thyssen, and we support bringing this debate again and again back to this chamber, to the committees of parliament, since clearly we need much more discussion, sharing and vigorous action.

in writing. ‒ ladies and gentlemen, research shows that air pollutants can travel several thousand kilometres before they settle. therefore, problems must be solved at the international level. the convention on long-range transboundary air pollution, which entered into force in 1983, was the first international legally binding instrument in this field. to date, the convention has been extended by eight protocols setting out specific measures to reduce emissions of air pollutants such as sulphur and nitrogen oxides, volatile and persistent organic compounds, heavy metals, combat acidification, eutrophication and tropospheric ozone, introduce national ceilings and reduce emissions for various substances below 1990 levels. in december 2009, the protocol was amended to update the obligations of the parties and to reflect best available techniques. decisions to amend shall be subject to ratification by the parties. the amendments to the protocol are largely covered by eu legislation and will be further transposed by a new directive setting updated national ceilings for emissions of certain air pollutants. the ratification of the amendments will be an important step towards achieving a higher level of protection of human health and the environment from transboundary air pollution. that is why i voted to give parliament its approval.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the application of the safeguard clause and the anti-circumvention mechanism providing for the temporary suspension of the application of the tariff preferences under the association agreement between the european union and the european atomic energy community and their member states, of the one part, and the republic of moldova, of the other part. the agreement establishes a preferential trade regime a deep and comprehensive free trade area (dcfta). in 2014, following the entry into force of the deep and comprehensive free trade agreement, imports into the union from moldova increased by 20%, while imports of agricultural goods increased particularly significantly, by 30%. agricultural products represent a significant share of the total imports from moldova to the union. the main exports of the union to moldova are spirits, food products and cigarettes. the reason to support the proposal is that a safeguard measure is required when, as a result of the reduction or elimination of the duty on a product originating in the republic of moldova, imports of that product into the union are made in such increased quantities as absolute value or in comparison with the union production that they cause or threaten to cause 'serious injury' to the union industry.
in writing. statistics show that in 2014, following the entry into force of the deep and comprehensive free trade agreement, imports into the union from moldova increased by 20%, while imports of agricultural goods increased significantly, by 30%. agricultural products represent a major share of the total imports from moldova to the union. the products of moldovan agriculture, which is a traditional livelihood, are also known for their good quality in the regions of the republic inhabited by ethnic bulgarians and citizens with a bulgarian identity. for these reasons, i supported the present proposal on the application of a safeguard clause in the framework of the association agreement between moldova and the eu. i also believe that such mechanisms provide protection both for european producers in the event of abuse of the preferential arrangements and for local producers. by a similar mechanism, they are also protected in the event of artificially created competition through regulated imports from third countries. i support the policy of good trade relations between the european union and its immediate neighbours, but i also believe that this must be done without jeopardising the livelihoods of european farmers.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the implementation of the anti-circumvention mechanism providing for the temporary suspension of the tariff preferences under the association agreement between the european union and the european atomic energy community and their member states, of the one part, and georgia, of the other part. the commission has also taken into account the fact that the proposed regulation is not binding on the union and that the union is not bound by the provisions of the eu-georgia association agreement. the adoption of the proposed regulation is necessary in order to comply with georgia's obligations under the non-circumvention provisions of the agreement, in order to protect eu producers where necessary.
in writing. the european union is georgia's largest trading partner, with 27% of the caucasian republic's trade with the eu. on the other hand, trade with georgia accounts for 0.1% of eu trade. the association agreement between the european union and georgia was signed in may 2014 and entered into force provisionally on 1 september 2014. it contains a clause providing for the temporary suspension of the application of tariff preferences to georgian imports into the european union of goods listed in 'annex ii-c (e) ' to the agreement, in the event that imports of those goods and products reach excessive levels that are disproportionate to the current production capacities of georgian agriculture. given that, according to the statistics, georgian imports do not threaten european farmers and producers, including those in my country bulgaria, even in these difficult times for a number of sectors, i have today given my support to the european commission's proposal. by taking this step, europe is showing solidarity and supporting the development of its neighbours and partners. this is a basis for stability and a model that should be applied to all neighbours, because stability in our neighbourhood is a prerequisite for the prosperity of all europeans.

in writing. ‒ the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities recognises the right to education (article 24) and the right to participate in cultural life (article 30) without discrimination and on the basis of equal opportunities. at the same time, only 5% of all books published in developed countries and less than 1% in developing countries are in accessible reading formats, with over 26 million visually impaired people in europe alone. the marrakesh treaty establishing an international legal framework guaranteeing the application of limitations or exceptions to copyright for the benefit of persons who are blind was signed on 27 june 2013. its signing raised doubts that the issue of blindness was being used to weaken copyright protection overall, which negatively affected the ratification process. my colleagues in the european parliament and i adopted a resolution on the ratification of the marrakesh treaty as soon as possible. seven eu member states are in the blocking minority and are obstructing the ratification process. i join the european parliament in calling for laws protecting intellectual property rights not to serve as an unjustified barrier to access to cultural materials by people with visual impairments.

author. mr president president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the island regions of the european union have common and specific permanent characteristics and peculiarities which clearly distinguish them from the continental territories. article 174 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union expressly recognises that island regions as a whole are characterised by persistently unfavourable conditions. as indicated in the sixth report on economic, social and territorial cohesion, the impact of the crisis has seriously affected the development potential of many disadvantaged regions, including island regions. the islands of the european union are also peripheral regions situated on the external borders of the union. this makes them particularly vulnerable to the challenges currently facing europe, such as globalisation, demographic trends, climate change, energy supply, and in particular in the southern regions, exposure to increasing migration flows. the connectivity of island regions to the mainland is a key factor in developing their full potential. therefore, particular emphasis in their development should be placed on transport links, intermodal transport and sustainable mobility, as well as on the development of digital capacity, which is vital to offset the disadvantages of connectivity. these and other factors should lead the eu to adopt specific measures to improve the social, economic and territorial cohesion of island regions. however, in preparing the 2014-2020 programming period, eu island regions did not receive any specific funding, only the possibility to modulate the co-financing rates for certain types of islands. in this context, on behalf of the committee on regional development, i would like to ask the european commission: can the european commission provide a clear definition of the type of permanent adverse natural or demographic conditions under article 174 tfeu that island regions are expected to face at nuts 2 and nuts 3 level? what specific cohesion policy instruments and resources are available to address the handicaps arising from the insularity of these territories? what action will the commission take in the future with regard to compliance with article 174 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union as regards the recognition of the persistent disadvantages faced by island regions at nuts 2 and nuts 3 level as permanent obstacles that may affect the achievement of the objectives of cohesion policy? does the european commission consider that indicators other than gdp, which go beyond the measurement of economic output and take into account the specificities of islands, such as the regional competitiveness index, could be taken into account in order to better reflect the economic and social vulnerability due to the persistent adverse natural conditions faced by these regions? i await the commission's answers.
