in writing. ‒ i supported the report by mrs kuneva, which proposes the recognition and professionalisation of domestic work and care for the elderly or sick, which, if achieved at european level, would help many of our fellow citizens in europe, because their work should be valued and properly paid. the report also deals extensively with various forms of violence and the risks associated with domestic work. it encourages member states to incentivise employers in the field of domestic work through subsidies or tax breaks and calls for a strengthened role of the european platform against undeclared work (currently serving as a platform for sharing and exchanging information). i believe that the subject can be addressed at european level and the report is a good step to offer the commission a more substantial analysis of the subject and possible proposals.
in writing. ‒ ladies and gentlemen, i support the report on female domestic workers and carers in the eu, as i believe it focuses attention on a particularly vulnerable group of labour market participants who need additional protection. the exploitation of labour in the eu continues to exist. according to the fundamental rights agency, domestic work and care work are among the sectors with the highest risk of labour exploitation in the european union. over 88% of those employed in these sectors are women, often employed on the basis of verbal contracts. in the absence of a formal contract, they are deprived of basic labour rights such as the right to paid annual leave, sick or maternity leave, insurance and pension rights, irregular remuneration, irregular working hours. better regulation of domestic and care work is needed in national legislation and measures at european level are needed to combat unregulated work in these sectors, and i believe that the report is an important step in this direction.
in writing. ‒ i supported the resolution because it is in the best interests of more than 2.5 million eu citizens, who work in the domestic work sector, to promote professional recognition of the skills and qualifications of domestic workers and carers. professionalization of the domestic work and care sector will not only increase the level of services provided but also will certainly create more jobs in this growing sector because there will be a place for professional development. in this regard, the commission should work extensively with the member states to find a common way to develop and recognise the skills of domestic workers, in particular of women domestic workers and carers. in addition, it is important to note that women are very vulnerable as domestic workers and carers, therefore they are victims of mental and physical abuse. in this context, the commission should work with member states to prevent violations and abuse and to protect their rights.
in writing. – employment and social rights are fundamental rights for every citizen of the european union. when around 2.5 million people who are domestic workers in the eu do not have rights because there is a lack of protection by the relevant institutions or laws, then it is our duty to change these institutions and laws. that is why i voted in favour of the resolution.
in writing. - gender equality is something that i and the imro have always supported, and i believe that the results achieved so far in our society are not to be underestimated. i will continue to work in this direction because i believe that capacity and skills are important in occupying a certain professional position and that gender is irrelevant and that discrimination in this regard must be stopped. and most importantly, the pay for a given position should not be different depending on gender. there are professions where women are more talented than men, and vice versa. there are more women in the relevant positions, which is normal. the decision to introduce quotas to increase the opportunities for women to occupy higher positions is not right for me and my political party, and it is only because of this reference in the text that i have abstained.
in writing. ‒ ladies and gentlemen, i support the report on gender equality and empowering women in the digital age. i believe that digitalisation has fundamentally changed the way people receive and provide information, communicate, learn and work, and this has a major impact on the labour market and creates new job opportunities and more flexible working patterns for women and girls in the ict sector. this in turn can help to empower them financially and give them independence and lead to a reduction in the overall gender pay gap. the participation of women in the information society is not only a matter of fairness and equality, but also contributes to the improvement of social and economic conditions in society and to the eu's competitiveness.
in writing. ‒ there is no doubt that the ict industry is the fastest growing sector of the world’s economy. therefore, the eu’s ‘digital agenda’ for growth, mobility and employment is a central pillar of the europe 2020 strategy. it is important to note that due to differences in demand and skills the eu may lack ict workers in 2020. to fill this gap, we should encourage more women to enter the digital jobs market. nowadays only 6% of ict developers in europe are women, only 19% of bosses in the ict and communications sectors are females (compared with 45% in other service sectors) and women represent just 19% of ict entrepreneurs (compared with 54% in other service sectors). looking from this perspective it could be argued that empowering women in the tech sector will provide not only a boost to the economy but also, and perhaps most importantly, will allow their full participation in society.
in writing. – the 2030 agenda for sustainable development, which was adopted by un member states in september, identifies icts as key enablers of growth and as an essential component of transformative solutions to meet today’s societal challenges. we must not miss the opportunity to close the persistent gender digital gap: in access, in usage, in content, in leadership and in opportunities in icts for women. the gender gap in icts has to be addressed in various dimensions of access, affordability, skills and usage, and only by closing the digital gender gap shall we be able to realise the full potential of icts as a catalytic and transformative tool for development and sustainable growth. in my work as an mep i support digital skills education and getting more girls interested in stem subjects, in coding and in programming to motivate the next generation of european women inventors and innovators. this is, i believe, essential to establishing the eu as a key driver of innovation, entrepreneurship and digital leadership. that is why i supported the report.
the rapporteur. madam president, what was the purpose of this report? with this report, we have tried to find another focus in cohesion policy and to increase its added value with a new approach to one of europe's most important assets: the mountains. mountains, which represent about 30% of the territory of the european union and nearly 17% of its citizens. i would like to take this opportunity to thank my colleagues from all political groups for the excellent work we have done together to reach this balanced text. what have we achieved in this document? we share the idea of the need to create a programme for the development of mountain regions. a european approach can do much to bring them closer together, especially if their advantages and disadvantages as separate territories are taken into account. this programme could eventually develop into a strategy for europe's mountains, which is part of the cohesion policy. secondly, we advocate the revision and coordination of the instruments existing at european level which have a bearing on mountains and the future integration of the mountain dimension in the regional and other policies of the european union. many union programmes, policies and instruments have a significant indirect role in mountains and the results they achieve can be enhanced if the mountain dimension is seriously addressed in them. thirdly, it is good that mountains are planned in the next programming period after a european definition has been established and put into the next regulation. defining the mountains of europe is a difficult task and many similar definitions exist even in european documents. but in the common agricultural policy, the definition of mountains is laid down in the regulation itself, which is also necessary in cohesion policy, in order to put a special emphasis on mountain agriculture. why is such a policy necessary? firstly, mountains have specific characteristics, which are due to their difficult accessibility and vulnerability to climate change. at the same time, they have a wealth of resources and real potential for development. the report therefore focuses on environmental protection and the fight against climate change. this is the most important for all the mountains in europe, as it has an effect on tourism and agriculture in many of them. mountains are an excellent source of all types of renewable energy - wind, solar, water and biomass. they provide an excellent opportunity for the development of eu renewable energy policy, which can be concentrated in mountain regions. the economy of the mountains still depends heavily on crafts, tourism, and agriculture. we call for support for small and medium-sized enterprises with a separate approach to mountain regions, precisely to take account of these and other features. all this politics goes through education, which has its own specifics. during the preparation of my report, i saw a number of cases where dual education leads to good results, as in the mountains it is necessary to concentrate on skills and training, especially in sectors that do not lead to environmental pollution. last but not least, accessibility and connectivity are important. the links between mountains and their surrounding areas are key, as our proposal for a definition shows. high-quality internet is key, because without it we cannot facilitate the creation of small and medium-sized enterprises and the economic development of mountain regions. attracting so-called 'independent professionals', i.e. people whose workplace is not fixed, is a very realistic way of improving the demographic situation. i'll stop here and wait for your suggestions. i hope tonight we'll learn a lot of ideas and put them into practice.
author. madam president, commissioner, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, i present a question for oral answer and a draft resolution with the general title 'accelerating the implementation of cohesion policy'. the question for oral answer is directly related to the two reports presented previously and relates to the implementation of cohesion policy throughout the planning period. more than two years have passed since the start of the current cohesion policy programming period and we are already experiencing serious delays in its implementation. there were delays in the adoption of operational programmes, there were delays in the implementation and implementation of a significant number of preconditions laid down in the member states' partnership agreements, there were delays in the designation of the competent programme and certification bodies by the member states. this is why we can generally observe delays in the start of implementation of the programmes and in the preparation and submission of payment documents. the commission notes that the commission has not provided any evidence that the measures in question are imputable to the state. over the years, the european parliament has often called on the european commission to respond appropriately to the problem of the delay in the implementation of cohesion policy. an example of this was the debate on the sixth cohesion report held in this chamber. in this context, we have repeatedly stressed the crucial importance of simplifying policy, good governance and coordination and synergies with other policies and their financial instruments. meps welcomed the establishment of a working group on better implementation of the 2007-2013 programmes in eight member states and the establishment by the commission of a high-level group of independent experts on simplification. despite all this, more efforts are needed to overcome the serious challenges facing the european union's cohesion policy. parliament calls on the commission to make a detailed assessment of progress in the implementation of cohesion policy, to prepare an in-depth analysis of the risks of financial losses for member states in the event of cancellation of commitments, indicating the specific amounts per country, and to analyse the estimates of disbursements according to the documents submitted by member states. for these reasons, and on behalf of the committee on regional development, i would like to ask the european commission what concrete measures it has taken and will take to prevent losses in the event of cancellation of commitments. what measures are being and will be taken to ensure full implementation of the payment plan within the budget for 2016 and also for the following years of the plan period? what measures has it taken and what will it take to improve the administrative capacity at all levels for the implementation of cohesion policy? and last but not least: how will the european commission encourage the implementation of the appropriate structural reforms needed to implement cohesion policy effectively? finally, i would like to ask the commission what will be the focus of the work of the group on better programme implementation for the 2014-2020 programming period? the european parliament calls on the european commission, through the decisions of the committee on regional development, to respond to these questions and to provide parliament with a comprehensive assessment of the situation and the envisaged solutions with a view to the effective implementation of the european union's cohesion policy and to opening a debate on the future of cohesion policy, based on the experience gained in addressing the challenges of this period.
member of the commission.– mr president, on behalf of the european commission i would like to thank the honourable members iotova and tomašić for their reports and also the honourable members who participated in this debate. the legal and policy framework for the european structural and investment funds for 2014-2020 has entailed a major leap forward in taking account of the diversity of european regions, in particular their mountainous areas, and developing specific tools to exploit the potential of this diversity. for this new funding cycle, member states are required to set out in their partnership agreements an integrated approach to address the specific needs of geographical areas suffering from severe and permanent handicaps. furthermore, they have at their disposal new instruments to reflect these specificities. i have mentioned modulation of eu co-financing rates but also integrated territorial investments and community-led local development. the commission strongly believes that the introduction of these new territorial tools will facilitate promoting an integrated place-based approach to territorial development in cohesion policy as well as to foster a bottom-up approach. but, following the adoption of the esif programmes, now it is up to member states to take up these new tools and to translate our funds into to growth and jobs for european regions and european citizens. it is their responsibility, but the commission is actively supporting them in this endeavour. we are jointly examining those programmes where particular efforts are needed. we have set up a high-level group on simplification. we are supporting administrative capacity, providing a great deal of guidance so that they can accelerate implementation without having to compromise on quality. i noted that many mentioned capacity building, and it is worth mentioning the several administrative capacity building actions proposed by the commission in areas such as public procurement and state aid and the taiex-regio peer 2 peer platform designed to help officials involved in the management of the european regional development fund and the cohesion fund to exchange knowledge and to exchange good practices. also, the newly established structural reform support service will assist member states in carrying out structural reforms. it was also suggested that the commission needs to communicate its policies better such as fc and esif complementarities and the commission recently published a brochure on fc and esif complementarities which is available on the commission’s website as well as a technical website on the same topic. the commission is confident that this work will bear fruit, allowing investments to result and sustainable growth for people on the ground, which is after all our common objective to us all. i can assure you the commission will spare no energy in these efforts. finally, i would like to thank you very much for your very valuable comments and suggestions, which the commission duly notes.
the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank all my colleagues in this chamber for the high regard they have given to the report we produced together with the shadow rapporteurs on mountain regions. in fact, most of these statements reflect a great concern, and that is the concern about the depopulation of these regions in europe. this trend is not limited to the more peripheral countries, it's not limited to countries like bulgaria and romania, where entire mountain municipalities are disappearing. one of the most frightening statistics i came across in my own country was that a quarter of the settlements in the mountain regions had no children under 14. although less so, the rich countries also show a trend of depopulation. with the loss of mountain communities, not only are the ecosystem services we all depend on being lost. the rich culture of the mountains is being lost, as well as the excellent opportunities for development. and that is why i want to address the european commission tonight. ladies and gentlemen, when you are preparing the new multiannual financial framework, when we are now making a general review of the current financial framework, let us pay special attention and emphasis to the mountain regions of europe. it is an inexhaustible resource for all of us, and future generations will not forgive us if we do not pay special attention to these regions now.
in writing. ladies and gentlemen, today a united europe is torn by dividing lines between member states, emerging in the way of solving old and newly emerging crises. nord stream 2 is the project that draws a new dividing line. this time, the split is in the context of one of the eu's most significant initiatives for a new impetus to unite, namely the creation of a european energy union, in which solidarity and trust between the parties will achieve security and diversification of energy supplies and competitive prices in a common energy market. i would like to recall the abandoned but priority eu-wide nabucco project, whose fate was decided by the choice of another solution by the private companies concerned. is it possible today that the gas map of europe could be redrawn again by the consortium of european energy companies and gazprom involved in nord stream? will the eu's repeatedly declared priorities for the development of the southern gas corridor be relegated to the background again? can governments do anything? perhaps such questions would not be asked if information about why and to whom this project is needed were made publicly available. it is high time for a real openness in the european energy sector to trigger the solidarity and trust mechanism.
in writing. the link between economic growth and tackling high unemployment is undeniable. but to get young people into the labour market, we cannot rely solely on european youth employment programmes and state programmes. career prospects are driven by a stable and prosperous economy on the one hand and the upskilling and mobility of europeans on the other. the european economy is growing at about 2% a year, but according to the european commission's recent economic forecast, unemployment will fall by only half. that means we need to change our economic model, creating new opportunities for young people to be involved. promoting young entrepreneurs and providing traineeships and vocational training are at the heart of this new model, which not only boosts employment but also boosts the economy. it is also important to promote the development of business skills in the next four years, 16 million more jobs will require high-skilled people. and to make these people available everywhere in europe, we also need to improve professional mobility. the legal prerequisites for the free movement of labour are in place, but now is the time to overcome practical and administrative obstacles, creating a truly transparent labour market.
in writing. – international trade is key to building a worldwide economic network and enabling emerging economies to improve their situation. nevertheless international trade must be controlled and regulated to not allow unfair advantages for some individuals or businesses over others. i support the proposal concerning the amendments to ensure the appropriate and transparent application of the anti-subsidy and anti-dumping rules to guarantee fair competition between eu firms and their non eu competitors.
in writing. ‒ i decided to vote in favour of this report because i am convinced that a clearer framework of agreements and provisions is needed, especially when acting outside the eu. we must avoid unnecessary misunderstandings and legal loopholes to protect our fishing vessels and the transport of fish. more importantly, however, by better managing fisheries in the region, we indirectly protect the eu's fish resources and avoid market disruptions due to economic fluctuations and other damage, overpopulation, etc. although fishing waters are not directly linked to southern and eastern european waters, small changes in the marine ecosystem can have dangerous consequences for fishing in our waters, i.e. the mediterranean and black sea regions.
in writing. ‒ i support the eu-liberia sustainable fisheries partnership agreement and the protocol on its implementation. it will strengthen cooperation between the eu and liberia, but also more generally between the eu and west africa. the liberian authorities have also provided information on the fishing activities of the vessels involved in the illegal fishing activities in the liberian fishing zone. this reduces the potential to increase national income from fishing activities and has a negative impact on fish stocks and marine ecosystems. i believe that in the long run, eu financial support will have a positive impact on the local economy. the protocol will help to strengthen monitoring, control and surveillance and contribute to better fisheries management in the region. the conclusion of this agreement will help the eu to achieve its objectives in the fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing and to implement one of the priorities of the common fisheries policy sustainable management of fisheries and aquaculture. the protocol will bring greater security and more rights for eu vessels, thus strengthening its role in the region.
in writing. ‒ i supported the report on the cooperation agreement between the european union and the republic of korea on the global civil navigation satellite system, as i believe it is important for all citizens. the international nature of the galileo programme has led several countries to apply for a cooperation agreement with the european union. korea formally expressed its interest in march 2005. the european commission, on the basis of authorisation from the council, negotiated a global civil navigation satellite system cooperation agreement between the european community (and its member states) and the republic of korea, which was subsequently signed in september 2006.
in writing. – the republic of korea is a country with capabilities in space technology and applications. it is an active user of satellite navigation services in various sectors including transport, fleet management, science and geodesy. i voted in favour of the cooperation agreement on a civil gnss with korea to allow for a more globalised and open partnership with the republic of korea.
in writing. ‒ i supported the report on the new territorial development instruments under cohesion policy 2014-2020 because the new initiatives represent an opportunity for local stakeholders to benefit from funding streams and to plan targeted local initiatives. the bottom-up approach adopted implies greater involvement of local actors and better coordination and absorption of european structural and investment funds.
in writing. – every person on our planet is affected by their surroundings and environment. working together and developing new tools to tackle problems linked to territorial development is key to developing solid partnerships across europe and beyond. the integrated territorial instruments provide a flexible mechanism for formulating integrated responses to diverse territorial needs, without losing the thematic focus through which cohesion policy is linked to the europe 2020 strategy. therefore, i vote in favour of the new territorial development tools in cohesion policy 2014-2020.
in writing. ‒ i support any report that leads to more transparency. this is about foreign direct investment and how to distinguish it from mergers and/or acquisitions of existing companies. we have a case in our country in 2015 that was reported as the largest foreign investment for that year, and it wasn't. something has to change to avoid differences in the statistics and hence in the future plans of the community countries, because this can affect the economic growth of a country and hence of the union.
in writing. – in our globalised and digital world, information plays a key role in understanding the successes and failures of past events. the gathering of such information and the evaluation of statistics, especially concerning economic issues, is key to creating an innovative and successful market economy of the 21st century. i vote for the gathering of statistics concerning balance of payments, international trade in services and fdi to enable a better and more transparent analysis of the european economy. i am certain this will lead to a faster recognition of problems concerning global economic issues and a faster and more profitable decision making processes by investors.
in writing. ‒ i supported the report on the eu's cohesion policy for mountain regions because it focuses on the development needs of mountain regions in the european union and their potential to become sources of jobs and sustainable growth. mountain regions are crucial to achieving the eu's objectives of employment, cohesion and environmental protection through the sustainable use of their natural resources. mountain areas are generally disadvantaged because of their remoteness or extreme conditions, which can lead to lower social standards and increased unemployment, which requires the coordination of eu policies for these regions and, as indicated in the report, the establishment of a working definition of functional mountain areas in the context of cohesion policy to facilitate the coordination of policies and measures concerning these regions, as well as the creation of a specific approach for them due to their structural weaknesses. i believe that it is essential for better policy coordination and better strategic cooperation that the carpathians remain within the danube macro-regional strategy, because this guarantees participation in the enhanced cooperation framework, which generates new projects and cooperation networks.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report as it focuses on the opportunities that the eu's mountain regions provide for achieving the europe 2020 goals. it highlights the opportunities that mountain areas offer for job creation, sustainable tourism and the use of renewable energy sources. i welcome the call in the report for the creation of an eu programme for mountain areas. the integration of the mountain dimension into future eu programmes and policies, especially within the framework of the european structural and investment funds, is key to ensuring sustainable economic development of mountains. i believe that the coordination of eu policies for mountain areas ensures that eu funding has a clear strategic focus on achieving sustainable and inclusive growth. at the same time, i believe that the inclusion of the mountain-specific dimension in the framework of european territorial cooperation would provide a good direction for mountain policy in the eu by extending the platform for best practices in these areas. in conclusion, i support a coordinated approach to sustainable mountain development so that its enormous potential can be exploited to the full.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the cohesion policy in mountain areas in the eu, as i believe that it is essential for eu policies to have a specific approach to mountain areas, given their clear structural shortcomings. these areas need additional support to be able to provide long-term, not just seasonal, employment, economic development, prevention and management of natural disasters, and environmental protection. mountain regions should be included in all aspects of eu policies, including cohesion policy, through the introduction of a territorial impact assessment. it is crucial for many regions to identify solutions for access to quality education. in order to overcome the negative demographic trends in these countries, and in particular in the balkans, equal access to education and provision of childcare facilities, as well as adult training and retraining, would facilitate active integration into the labour market. last but not least, youth employment initiatives are a good opportunity to stem the outflow of young people in response to the demographic crisis and the problem of ageing populations in mountain regions.
in writing. ‒ 42% of the settlements in the mountain areas of bulgaria have fewer than 100 inhabitants, and 25% of them have no children under 14 years of age. the same levels of social and economic marginalisation of mountain areas are found in the carpathians and in the mountains of greece. today my colleagues in the european parliament and i adopted by a large majority a resolution on the eu's cohesion policy in mountain areas, which aims to secure additional targeted investment. the depopulation of these areas has led to the loss of real development opportunities. the demographic collapse that has affected all of europe is particularly pronounced there. providing better infrastructure in mountain areas is key to attracting new investment. the resolution addresses the above issues and focuses not only on agriculture and tourism as investment areas, but also on the potential for developing renewable energy based on water, wind, solar and biomass resources. the creation of employment through the subsidisation of small and medium-sized enterprises is also central to making mountain areas more attractive. i supported the adoption of the resolution because it is a step towards ensuring more favourable conditions for investment in the current and next programming period.
in writing. mountain regions are very important because of the opportunities and potential they have in solving local, national and global problems. however, worrying trends such as depopulation and population ageing are particularly acute in these countries. i therefore believe that we must look for ways and instruments, through the european cohesion funds, to halt and even reverse these trends. investments in closed-loop production are an opportunity for this. they ensure that the added value of the whole process remains in the region concerned. mountain farmers have a harder time matching the economic performance of their competitors in other regions due to transport, natural and other constraints. for this reason, i think they should look for ways to unite, and besides being able to offer more production and reduce the costs of each producer individually, this would also help them in negotiations with buyers. i support and call for the streamlining of administrative procedures for these producer organisations in the mountains. the lack of clarity and the lack of sufficient mechanisms to promote the 'mountain product' label at european level are still a fact. for this reason, it has not achieved the desired effect and recognition. in view of this, i strongly believe that the commission should propose financial instruments to promote it.
in writing. – the eu is built on a solid foundation of solidarity, trust and the idea that together we can achieve more than we could ever achieve alone. i vote for the cohesion policy in mountainous regions of the eu, to enable a more effective and productive environment for smes and other local businesses affected by environmental issues in mountainous regions.
in writing. ‒ ladies and gentlemen, i welcome the resolution on the eu's mountain cohesion policy, in which the ep calls for a pan-european programme for mountain regions as the basis for a future european strategy for their long-term development. mountains cover a significant part of the eu's territory (around 30%) and are at the heart of the protection of biodiversity and the fight against climate change. taking into account their cultural and natural heritage, mountain areas can become engines of 'green' and sustainable growth by developing a bio-economy based on agriculture, forestry, renewable energy, tourism and crafts. realising this potential requires a coordinated approach between the different eu policies and programmes in mountain areas to provide infrastructure for physical and digital accessibility, access to education, social services, health and development of multifunctional agriculture. in this context, i welcome the fact that the resolution covers the agri committee's proposals for 'revitalising' mountain areas through cap support for the development of mountain agriculture and livestock, including mountain dairy production. the establishment of the quality term 'mountain product', the support of agro-tourism and craft projects, as well as specialised training in these areas, will contribute to the preservation of the identity and cultural heritage of mountain areas.
madam president, the world humanitarian summit must outline a sustainable framework for humanitarian aid, designed for over 120 million people in need around the world. i hope that the results will surpass all previous donor conferences of a similar nature. one of the main issues to be raised at the meeting is the financing of humanitarian aid. as epp rapporteur in the shadow of the opinion of the subcommittee on human rights and as permanent rapporteur on recommendations to the un general assembly, i emphasised the priorities i would set during the meeting, namely: for more effective cooperation within the un system to cut recruitment and funding networks for terrorist groups, for the importance of interreligious and intercultural dialogue to reduce refugee flows, and for the allocation of financial and human resources for ongoing education in fundamental values such as human dignity, freedom of expression, equality and respect for the law. turkey, as the host of the meeting, must also respect basic democratic rules and not use this hosting for political propaganda purposes, but for the future of millions of needy people around the world. turkey was chosen to host this meeting before the wave of migration had yet to sweep the country and europe. there is something symbolic about the fact that the world is coming together for the first time in istanbul to come up with concrete solutions that will strengthen europe's role not only as the main donor of humanitarian aid but also as an active factor in shaping the development of the world.
in writing. we are facing a humanitarian crisis of unprecedented scale and nature. today, more than 400 million people worldwide are affected by armed conflicts, natural disasters, climate change and socioeconomic instability. these people need effective and secure humanitarian assistance. unfortunately, the provision and delivery of such assistance under the current system is a rather difficult undertaking due to the lack of funding and the lack of funds. that is why i believe that the world needs a new humanitarian system, one that is based on the fundamental principles of humanity, solidarity, the protection of human life and respect for the norms of international humanitarian law. it must rely on coordinated, timely and flexible funding, supported by a new public-private partnership. as the world's leading humanitarian aid donor, the eu has the potential and capacity to establish and develop such a humanitarian aid system. at the forthcoming world humanitarian summit in istanbul, the union must take the lead in bringing relief to the millions of suffering people. this is not only our moral duty, but also a commitment that the european union has continued to fulfil for decades.
madam president, mrs mogherini, i want to join in what you have said and express my respect for the efforts of jordan and lebanon to reduce the human suffering of millions in the region. the european union is the largest financial donor to the syrian crisis, having contributed to date over eur 5 billion from its own budget and from member states' budgets in the form of humanitarian aid and support for economic development and stabilisation. very often, we emphasize that turkey hosts over 2 million refugees, but we forget the small countries of lebanon and jordan, which have hosted a total of 1.7 million syrians, which is over 20% of their total population. in other words, the pressure on lebanon and jordan is enormous. we must not forget that in both countries there are also hundreds of thousands of palestinians and iraqis who have been displaced by other conflicts in the middle east. it is in our interest, not only in terms of values and humanity and compassion, but also in our interest to reduce the refugee flow to europe, to help both syria and jordan. after the agreement with the european union, europe must also help solve the refugee problem in other countries, but we must also turn to solutions within ourselves. with the changing world around us, with the crises in europe's neighbourhood, we need to be much more united and really go from being a so-called 'soft power' to becoming a 'hard power' to have a common defence capacity, to have common external border protection, common intelligence. in foreign policy, europe must be much more united and consolidated. i very much want, mrs mogherini, that we have a united voice before the world and that voice is your voice, that it is heard, that europe is respected and participates not only in humanitarian aid and development aid but also in finding political solutions to the crises around us.
in writing. what is happening in lebanon and jordan borders on a humanitarian catastrophe. it's no surprise that 65% of registered syrian refugees are under the age of 25. these people are fleeing mandatory military service, either in assad's army, or in the opposition free syrian army, or in the ranks of the islamic state. meanwhile, lebanon and jordan have severely restricted syrian refugees' ability to study and work legally, forcing them to rely solely on humanitarian aid and black-collar work. this is why the lives of syrian refugees in lebanon and jordan are a disaster, and humanitarian aid alone will not improve them. i believe that the european union should stop being just a donor of humanitarian aid and work with the countries that are hosting refugees to find ways to improve their lives. if that doesn't happen, i fear that many of the people who have fled to lebanon and jordan will be looking for ways to move to western europe.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by congratulating the rapporteur and the fictitious rapporteurs on their work on this proposal for a directive. the agreement reached with the council makes it possible to clarify and improve the conditions for trainees, volunteers, students and pupils from outside europe for the benefit of the union and its member states, as well as the countries of origin. i would like to emphasize three elements. firstly, this directive will have to be used by the member states to achieve the objectives of europe 2020. the conditions for entry and residence for students and researchers in particular will encourage a more rapid internationalisation of our education systems. it is about making the union more attractive, more competitive and achieving a europe of knowledge and innovation: that is our objective, and we are taking a real step forward today. another important and welcome feature of the text is that it sets out measures to ensure better protection for trainees by giving a member state the possibility to ensure that the traineeship does not replace a job. finally, i would like to call for this new directive to be taken into account in the framework of the european neighbourhood policy. education, research and the promotion of cultural exchanges remain objectives and means of building bridges between europe and its neighbours, in particular with the mediterranean region. this directive makes perfect sense when applied to our neighbours. it is a mutual investment between us and our neighbours, especially for young people, and we know how crucial it is to provide opportunities for young people in some of our neighbouring countries. i am glad that we can conclude this dossier and encourage a smart, controlled policy and circular migration here.
i welcome the forthcoming decision of the european parliament. europe should be home to all the smart, young scientists and innovators. the european commission has launched a new initiative to promote the integration of refugees into the european union. but what do we do about the brain drain inside the european union? my homeland bulgaria is a victim of emigration. millions of young and intelligent bulgarians were driven abroad by hunger and misery and became part of the intellectual elite of britain, france, spain and other european countries. but we also need to be careful about the necessary safeguards for european nations. we must selectively admit to europe only those students and scientists who are sure to increase our intellectual potential and the high-tech industries for which there is a shortage of labour.
mr president, in the current migration crisis, we often forget that, apart from illegal immigrants and refugees, europe is also attractive for highly qualified staff from third countries. the ageing population and the shortage of skilled labour are worrying in terms of the need to develop the information technologies, the digital market and research that are to be the future of the european economy. the conditions must therefore be created to attract the best talent in the world. i therefore welcome the agreement reached with the council on facilitating the travel of students and researchers from third countries within the european union. given the cross-border nature of much research and the joint work of a number of european research centres, such facilitated mobility is of paramount importance not only for scientists but above all for the development of european science. at the same time, of course, we must not overlook the need to find jobs for the millions of unemployed european citizens - especially young people - and to create the conditions for them to set up a thriving european business and find work that matches their qualifications and abilities. as european legislators, it is our duty to protect the interests and rights of european citizens in particular, and that is why i once again call for respect for the right to free movement within the european union without applying discriminatory measures or treatment to citizens of certain member states.
in writing. ‒ we cannot force one or another sector to comply with a regulation or directive before it has passed the scrutiny of that sector. yes, we do need to get investment brokers to comply with our legislation, but only after the audit is over. it may be that 31 december 2020 is a long way off, but it is better to do the audit well and not put time pressure on the auditors so that they can do their job properly.
in writing. – regulation 575/2013 exempts commodity dealers from large exposure requirements and from own funds requirements until 31 december 2017. it also requires the commission to prepare reports by 31 december 2015 on the prudential supervision of commodity dealers and of investment firms in general. applying large exposure requirements and own funds requirements to commodity dealers should not come as the result of a lapsed exemption but on the basis of a thoroughly reasoned decision. therefore i vote for the proposal extending the capital requirements exemption for commodity dealers under the capital requirements regulation (crr).
in writing. ‒ i supported the report by mrs diaz de mero because i believe that the proposed regulation provides a clear and comprehensive legal basis for europol, which broadens its powers and in practice enables it to tackle and respond more effectively to the challenges we face today. i also support the proposal in the new regulation that introduces a mechanism that provides for europol to be subject to scrutiny by the european parliament together with the national parliaments. i believe that europol needs to become more effective in the support it provides to member states to fight terrorism and to tackle all forms of organised and serious crime.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report because it provides for a strengthening of europol's mandate and a significant improvement in the agency's leverage to counter the increasing cross-border crime and terrorist threat. i am very pleased that the new rules will allow europol to respond more quickly and effectively to new security threats. for example, the agency will be able to exchange information directly with private entities such as companies or ngos to more quickly remove terrorist propaganda online. i welcome the agreement reached, as it will also help to avoid any gaps in the information needed to ensure the security of european citizens. to this end, the new rules oblige eu member states to provide europol with the information it needs to carry out its tasks. at the same time, guarantees for enhanced data protection and parliamentary scrutiny are provided, which go hand in hand with europol's new powers. i consider it to be a very democratic decision to have europol's work monitored by the joint parliamentary scrutiny group, composed of members of national parliaments and the european parliament. there is also a clear procedure for citizens' complaints under eu law.
in writing. ‒ there is a general feeling that the european union needs measures to ensure the security of its citizens. strengthening europol's mandate is a step in that direction. the texts adopted enhance the agency's capacity to counter terrorism and serious organised crime. it also improves europol's accountability to the european parliament and to the parliaments of the member states and lays down clear rules on the exchange of information between services and measures to protect personal data. the new legal framework will allow europol to respond more quickly to modern threats, such as the tools to tackle terrorist propaganda online. we are witnessing a new impetus in european integration towards ever closer and more effective cooperation in the field of policing. i do not hide my support for the creation of strong european institutions in the so-called area of freedom, security and justice of the european union.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the oral question to the commission with a motion for a resolution on accelerating the implementation of cohesion policy. cohesion policy is part of the eu's regional policy and aims to create jobs, business competitiveness, economic growth and sustainable development. the funds allocated to cohesion policy for the period 2014-2020 represent one third of the eu budget, but its implementation, as well as that of the related operational programmes, has been extremely slow. the commission is invited to accelerate the simplification process in order to help member states to improve the absorption of funds and to improve their administrative capacity.
in writing. ‒ the cohesion policy is eu’s main investment and development policy that covers all eu regions. by enhancing social and economic cohesion it aims to bring the eu closer to its citizens. having said that, in order for all regions to become competitive and to facilitate investment, we should accelerate the implementation of the cohesion policy. timely implementation is the key not only for the successful fulfilment of the europe 2020 strategy, in which the cohesion policy is a central pillar, but also to avoid member states’ decommitment of funds. it is important to note that achieving timely implementation will require administrative capacity building both at national and regional level. therefore, the commission should support the strengthening of member states’ administrative capacity. we should launch effective communication policy in order to raise public awareness of cohesion policy implementation so people to gain a better understanding of the results and impacts of cohesion policy.
in writing. with a budget of almost €350 billion by 2020, cohesion policy is an important investment and development mechanism in the eu, and in some member states it is the main source of public investment. at the same time, however, the information indicates that, although two years have already passed since the beginning of the current programming period, there are delays in the implementation of cohesion policy. by supporting this resolution, i join the call to the european commission to make full use of the opportunities offered by the european structural and investment funds to strengthen social cohesion between the different european regions and to reduce the territorial disparities to which delays in the funds are detrimental. an important finding from the previous period is that administrative capacity at national, but also at regional and local level, is a key precondition for the successful implementation of cohesion policy and for increasing the competitiveness of regions. i therefore believe that the european commission should support the strengthening of administrative capacity for the policy implementation phases.
mr president, the events of the past few months have shown that the european asylum system as it stands cannot cope. europe was facing an unprecedented crisis that placed a disproportionate burden on several countries. it turned out that the temporary protection directive, created specifically to deal with sudden migratory flows, could not be applied as it did not provide for a mechanism for mandatory responsibility sharing. we must learn the right lessons from this experience. we need a comprehensive reform of the system that ensures genuine european solidarity, not measures that are unable to deal with the problems in the long term. while the commission proposal does not envisage a centralised european system, the automatic application of a corrective allocation mechanism for asylum seekers is a step in the right direction. i therefore call on the council to support the proposed amendment in the interests of finding a more long-term solution.
in writing. the current dublin mechanism needs to be amended to ensure a fair distribution of responsibilities between member states. the frontline countries should not bear a disproportionate burden, investing significant resources and bearing sole responsibility for the protection of the eu's external border. a new mechanism must be able to work in the long term, not just to overcome the current crisis. it is also important to take into account the lessons learned from the implementation of relocation and resettlement mechanisms. the right to protection must be guaranteed, but at the same time the possibilities for abuse must be avoided. this means clearly distinguishing between those who are fleeing war and those who are entering the eu illegally. all common action in the field of migration policy should be based on the principle of solidarity and fair sharing of responsibilities.
the events of 2015, namely the unprecedented number of migrants and the terrorist attacks in paris, have shown that the actions taken so far to manage the external borders of the european union are not effective in addressing today's challenges. more importantly, events have demonstrated the invariable link between the need to protect the external borders of the european union and the preservation of the free movement of people within the european union and schengen. i believe that the legislative proposals currently under discussion, such as the european border guard, will lead to better and more efficient management of external borders, and the most important thing is to ensure a pan-european approach rather than individual action by member states. only in this way will it be possible to guarantee the integrity and the future of the schengen area. i want to emphasize here that the european union and schengen will be more secure if bulgaria is accepted as a member of schengen as soon as possible. as the european external border, we are responsible for ensuring the security not only of bulgarian citizens, but also of all over 500 million europeans. the work of the bulgarian border police in combating foreign fighters and illegal migration across european borders has proven to be extremely successful and is often held up as an example. i can safely say that bulgaria is better at protecting its borders than some schengen members. acceptance of the country in schengen and providing full access to the relevant information systems will inevitably contribute to greater european security. the future of schengen depends on our willingness to take more european action, and that includes bulgaria's admission to schengen.
madam president, the schengen area is one of the most significant achievements of modern europe. it guarantees the free movement of hundreds of millions of citizens of the european union. however, in the past year, six schengen members have reintroduced internal border controls for reasons related to the refugee crisis. this temporary introduction of border controls has a negative impact on trade, but above all it has important implications for the european project, expressed in euroscepticism, anti-immigrant and populist rhetoric. i therefore believe that we must restore the normal functioning of the schengen area by the end of this year at the latest. to do this, we need to ensure the protection of the european union's external borders, and this can be achieved with the newly created european border and coast guard. it should be based on shared responsibility and solidarity, and member states which are not yet part of the schengen area, such as bulgaria and romania, should also participate in it. i believe that returning to the normal functioning of the schengen area is a return to the foundations of european integration.

in writing. ‒ china is our second largest trading partner, while the eu is china's largest, with an average daily trade of over one billion euros. at the same time, out of all 75 anti-dumping measures in force in the eu, 56 are against chinese imports. in practice, the eu acknowledges the existence of a state dumping policy on chinese exports, but it must further strengthen the protection of the european industry against such unfair practices. the chinese state's intervention with subsidies and other support to form non-market prices in exports is sufficient evidence of the absence of market economy status not only by european criteria but also by wto criteria. i call for all acceptable and lawful solutions to be found to prevent the european economy from being further exposed to the dangers of china's non-market trade practices, which threaten to lose hundreds of thousands of jobs in various industrial sectors. the overcapacity in china today, which is many times greater than the production capacity of the european steel, ceramic, glass, solar panels, etc. sectors, is a real threat to our economy with significant economic and social consequences, including massive job and business closures. the eu cannot afford for this to happen.

member of the commission. – mr. president, i am very grateful to have this opportunity to discuss the important issue of foreign currency loans. taking out a mortgage to buy a home is the single biggest financial transaction that most people undertake in their lives. so we need a vibrant and competitive mortgage market, one where people have choice, but also one where they know what they are buying and what risks they are taking on. one of the products that became popular in recent years was loans made in foreign currencies, and for many years they offered consumers low interest rates. but recent experience has shown that they can become a problem if they are offered to households that cannot protect themselves properly against sudden changes in exchange rates, and here i think loans in swiss francs, provide a good example. these have been popular in countries like croatia, poland, hungary and romania. but when the swiss national bank stopped pegging swiss francs to the euro in january last year, the cost of servicing those mortgages shot up and that left households struggling to keep up with their mortgage repayments, which in turn put pressure on governments to take action to help those who were in difficulty. some countries have already passed laws; others are considering doing so. in terms of what the commission has done for the future, we have acted to ensure that risks associated with foreign currency loans are better managed by strengthening consumer protection in the mortgage credit directive. but that does not deal with the problem of the existing loans in foreign currencies, and here we are working closely with governments that are considering how best to respond. of course, there is a need to protect the interests of consumers, but we also need to make sure that any measures taken are fully consistent with the single market and that they do not restrict disproportionately the free movement of capital or the freedom of european companies to do business anywhere in the eu. we also have to consider the potential damage that would be done to investor confidence if we were to undermine legal certainty. croatia has chosen to pass legislation that allows borrowers to convert swiss-franc loans into euro-denominated loans at an exchange rate that pre-dates the franc's appreciation. it puts borrowers in the position that they would have been had they initially chosen a euro-denominated loan, but it places the cost of the conversion, a cost that i understand is some eur 1 billion, almost wholly on the shoulders of the banks that issued the loans without regard to the different circumstances of the borrowers. the commission was not consulted on the draft legislation, and the croatian government was under no obligation to do so. since its adoption, we have assessed whether croatia's amendments to its consumer credit act and the credit institutions act are compatible with the principles of the single market. let me give you our initial analysis. it is clear that the goal of protecting borrowers to avoid a debt crisis can justify restrictions to the free movement of capital or the freedom of establishment, but in our view, allowing borrowers to exchange their loans from swiss francs into euros at an artificially low exchange rate and placing the cost almost exclusively on lenders goes beyond what is needed to avoid a crisis and protect those borrowers. there is clearly a problem that needs tackling, so we need to find a proportionate solution in line with treaty freedoms and one that helps maintain investor confidence in croatia. the issue has been discussed at the ecofin council. we are monitoring the situation carefully in croatia, but also in other countries that are currently considering passing legislation. we are keeping all options open, including of course opening an infringement procedure if that proves necessary. we are in close contact with the croatian government, who tell us that they are keen to find a way forward and they are talking to the banks concerned to find a more balanced approach that shares the burden of adjustment more fairly. i support that approach, but clearly there must be progress soon or we will have to take appropriate action. so, we need a solution that strikes the right balance, one that is consistent with eu legislation, that protects consumers but also investment and the single market. that is the solution that i will continue to push for, and that is what i want to see in every member state where this is currently a matter of concern.
on behalf of the ecr group. mr president, commissioner, i cannot help but note that foreign currency loans are extremely widespread in some member states. in particular, swiss franc loans were popular in the recent past in eastern european countries, where about 60% of outstanding loans were taken in foreign currency. the data show that foreign currency loans are mainly held by european households, with a relatively small share held by the corporate and government sectors. it is also noteworthy that only in the united kingdom and luxembourg is a large percentage of loans in swiss francs made to persons who are nationals of other countries, reflecting the status of these countries as international financial centres. the attractiveness of foreign currency loans lies in their immediate benefits, such as lower interest rates and longer repayment terms. however, they carry a lot of risks, as households do not expect to have income in the relevant foreign currency or to be protected from the exchange rate risk. as i mentioned earlier, a few years ago in central and eastern europe, the popularity of loans in foreign currencies, particularly swiss francs, increased because interest rates were much lower in switzerland. people took advantage of these loans to buy real estate. in 2008, however, the value of many of the currencies collapsed against the franc, putting the borrowers in a situation where they had to pay back in local currency an amount many times higher than the value of the loan. as of 2008, bulgarians are the world's top borrowers of foreign currency, with home loans being the most popular. however, according to analyses conducted last autumn, 99% of bank loans are in leva or euros, as these currencies are considered stable and are not expected to be affected by the changes taking place in international markets. while in the 1990s, loans in dollars or francs were popular among my compatriots, since bulgaria's accession to the eu, a large number of businesses and households have benefited from the integration of our country's economy into the european economy and are increasingly using the euro and the lev. this is due not only to the security of the euro but also to the protection that european law affords its citizens. in particular, the unfair terms directive and the case law of the court of justice of the european union provide for a set of rules to replace unfair terms in similar foreign currency credit agreements.

vice-president of the commission. – mr president, honourable members of the european parliament, thank you very much for this really fruitful debate. according to my understanding, all the services provided by our governments had to be digital by default, open by default and cross-border by default. we all know that those e-governmental services will make our governments more efficient, more transparent, which is extremely important, but if those services are provided in a really transparent way, then this will not create the best environment for corruption for example. not everybody will be happy about this, and also those governments which will provide internet-based services are, as a rule, more inclusive governments. but to involve our people it is extremely important. it is important by the governments to provide their citizens with a single digital identity, and this identity has to be strong, because this is all about trust. once again, if people do not trust those internet-based e-services, they will never start to use those services. about efficiency. single digital identity makes those governmental services but also private services cheaper than usage of traditional signatures. so it is not polite to provide examples always about estonia. but in estonia we think that just because of usage of digital signatures, we were able to save one working week per year, which is equal to 2% of our gdp, which is equal to our defence expenditure. we can say defence expenditure in estonia is coming from digital signatures. so it is a question about efficiency. i would like also to underline the importance of the ‘once only’ principle. i know once again from my own experience how important it was to introduce this ‘once only’ principle. in estonia it took six years to get those first one million digital signatures and then we introduce, the ‘once only’ principle. it means the state has the right to ask for information from their citizens or their companies only once, and it gave a real boost on usage of those digital identities. now, in the country i know best, they are getting more than 1.3 million digital signatures per week already, and the population in estonia is 1.3 million inhabitants. all those digital solutions provided by our governments had to be user-centric, and if those solutions included digital identities, they will be really user-centric solutions, then people they will use those solutions. if signing digitally will take four or five minutes, nobody will start to use those solutions. there are some really good examples. for example, in austria i know people they are using mobile identities quite often, in some other countries also, it is common to use mobile identities instead to use those smart id cards. those solutions, digital solutions, they have to be user-centric and then people they will use those solutions and our people they have to be absolutely sure that those solutions are there, also really safe and well protected. it is true that our registers do not talk with each other. we have in all the countries digital prior business registers, but it is very difficult to get information in a digital way, in a trusted manner, from another country from those business registers. if somebody wants to make business for example here in belgium, but he is coming from some other countries, then how those local people they know who has mandate to represent this company here in this country? it is so easy theoretically to get information from business register, but in real life paper is needed. in the 21st century paper is still needed for that. we have some quite good examples about the regional cooperation, about mutual recognition of digital identities – i know best about this example we have in the baltic states and between finland also – but there are some other examples also. we have already eidas directive which allows mutual recognition of those digital identities, but full implementation of eidas directive takes some time. we have implementation acts. there is cooperation networking in place. the eidas observatory will be launched in the second half of 2016 to boost online trust security and transparency in the digital single market and to facilitate the use of cross-border electronic identification and trust services. but i absolutely agree with those people who say that the european commission has to lead by example, and we will try to do that. so e-procurement it is a real challenge for all of us. according to analysis prepared by the european parliament, if we will be able to use e-procurement across the european union, we can save one billion euros per year. but also this service is based on strong digital identities. in the european commission we have to be ready for full implementation of e-procurement. about organised crime and the refugee crisis. once again, single digital identity based on biometrics is needed. as we know, just recently it happened so that one of those terrorists was able to change his identity in the european union even 7 times. it is a shame. so we have to build up really good interoperability network and we have to introduce in all the eu member states strong digital identities, and we have to fully implement the eidas directive. i am looking forward to really fruitful cooperation in this field between the european commission and the european parliament.
in writing. – i believe that the shift to e-government in europe through the development of e-identification tools and a wide availability of online services is a very important milestone in the development of the digital single market and the future of the european union. it is essential for competitiveness, reducing costs for businesses and making life easier for european citizens and therefore requires ambitious initiatives. in order to ensure the adoption of online services, the deployment of a secure digital identity is necessary to build public trust and ensure convenience. in this respect, we need to support the initiatives for promoting awareness about the opportunities of e-identification. a secure electronic identification is an important step towards data protection and the prevention of online fraud. citizens and businesses need to be able to trust that their data is treated in full respect of existing data protection legislation. without certainty on the legal validity of all these related services, businesses and citizens will remain reluctant to use the digital interactions as their natural way of interaction because they will be unsure of the issue of a possible dispute.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, putting citizens at the heart of the energy union and tackling energy poverty deserves our full attention and thank you very much for the report. the report is very timely because the energy transition and the new technologies are changing how the energy markets work. this can and must bring benefits to all consumers, be it households or industry. however, it is a fact that retail markets for energy are not working today for consumers as they should. consumer satisfaction and engagement in the energy market remain persistently low, and we have seen a trend of rising energy prices for end-consumers across the eu. the new deal for energy consumers is about correcting these shortcomings. our objective is to deliver: a competitive, technology-driven and fair energy market which delivers high-quality energy services to consumers. this means removing barriers for companies with innovative products and services which try to enter the market. we want a market where consumers can make informed choices about the way they consume energy and about the sources of energy they want to consume. and we want a market-based framework to protect vulnerable consumers and fight energy poverty. in the short time that i have today, please let me mention a few issues to make this more concrete. we want bills to be clearer and easier to compare with alternative offers. therefore, we are analysing possibilities for an eu certification scheme for price comparison tools. we have to work on removing the barriers for switching between providers. barriers still exist and harm both consumers and innovative companies. i am pleased to see that parliament recognises the importance of smart technologies in the energy sector. technology costs are falling rapidly. this means that more and more consumers could reduce their energy bills by using technologies like rooftop solar panels, heat pumps or smart meters. demand response and storage solutions must be developed. this is beneficial for energy efficiency and for consumers. but, as rightly pointed out in the report, we need to put the necessary enabling legal framework in place. we must adjust our rules to the energy technologies of the 21st century. we need a better framework for decentralised generation and self-consumption. we need more cooperatives, aggregators, and energy service companies in order to ensure access for those who are not in a position to self-generate, such as tenants and vulnerable consumers. and finally, we need a better and informed debate about energy cost, taxes, levies and subsidies. therefore, we will publish in the second half of this year a report on energy prices and costs that will enhance transparency on the different components of energy prices in the member states. the cost of energy leads me to the second topic of today: energy poverty. let me mention a few figures. in 2014, approximately 10% of eu citizens felt that they were unable to keep their homes adequately warm. since 2000, the share of energy spending of the lowest income households in their total income increased from 6% to 9%, which means a 50% increase. this is significant for the small budgets that these households have. i know from my energy union tour and from the country analyses which we drew up, that we have a very diverse picture in europe but energy poverty is an issue everywhere. of course, well-targeted social policy measures are the most direct and effective tool to address poverty. this is, correctly, the competence of the member states. but nevertheless, the commission is analysing if and how our work can support the member states in addressing energy poverty. the fight against social exclusion and poverty is a cross-cutting policy issue, so let me mention just a few examples. we are analysing if a definition of energy poverty is possible and how it could help address the problem. with your support, thanks to your pilot project on fuel energy poverty, the commission is considering an energy poverty observatory. this will help us to quantify, monitor and identify best practices and we expect to launch this in 2018 following an open tender. we are working with the member states to share good practices. as an example, bulgaria was mentioned by our rapporteur and commissioner arias cañete is travelling just now to bulgaria to speak about the topic in the context of electricity market liberalisation, an area where the commission services have provided support to bulgaria in recent months. the commission agrees that energy efficiency is the most effective way to prevent energy poverty. it reduces greenhouse gas emissions and energy bills. it contributes to better health and living standard, and as for all energy efficiency measures, it creates jobs in the local economy. we have underlined the importance of energy poverty from the very beginning, and we promised in the first state of the energy union report that we would pay particular attention to the issue when reviewing key legislation in 2016. therefore, the report and the resolution which we discuss today are very timely. i would like to thank theresa griffin and all other colleagues involved in this for their work. i would also like to acknowledge the resolution on meeting the anti-poverty target in the light of increasing household costs which this parliament adopted on 14 april 2016. i can promise that we will examine all your recommendations on tackling energy poverty very closely. i am very much looking forward to this debate and i would like to thank you for giving me the floor.
